requirement: In a book chapter, each valid `{impl}`, `{cite}`, or `{test}` reference, inline or fenced, MUST render as a Shields.io static badge image with meaningful alt text that displays its role and full name and links to the badge at the corresponding `{req}` or `{example}` definition. Links MUST work across chapters, including nested chapters. A fenced reference MUST render its badge followed by its body as Markdown. Each fenced `{req}` or `{example}` directive MUST render as a Shields.io definition badge image identifying its kind; text outside a directive MUST remain literal. Badge text MUST remain legible regardless of whether its link has been visited. A badge link MUST show a visible indicator when it has keyboard focus and MAY brighten on hover. Badges MAY be laid out inline with the surrounding text, a fenced reference's badge and body MAY be visually set apart from the surrounding text as one block, and a built-in's unlinked badge MAY show a help cursor to signal its hover text. These badges use the syntax defined by {cite}`requirements.references.roles`.
rationale:
I found no gap against `requirements.references.book_badges`. Each obligation has code that carries it out and a test that asserts its outcome.

**Badge for each valid reference.** `src/lib.rs#fn[reference_badge]` builds the badge for a valid `{impl}`, `{cite}` or `{test}` reference.
- It calls `shield_badge`, which produces an `img.shields.io` image whose `alt` is "role fullname".
- It wraps the image in an `<a>` that links to the definition anchor, or in an unlinked `<span>` with the help text as `title` for built-ins.
- `{fixme}` and term targets return `None` and stay literal.
- `fn[replace_inline_references]` applies this to inline references, and `fn[replace_references]` applies it to fenced ones.
- Tests: `fenced_references_render_their_badge_and_body_and_built_ins_are_unlinked`, `references_in_nested_chapters_link_to_the_requirement_definition` (colors and alt/URL for impl, cite and test) and `shields_badge_urls_escape_requirement_names`.

**Links across chapters, including nested ones.**
- `fn[chapter_href]` computes relative `../` paths.
- `fn[replace_definitions]` emits the target `id="habeas-req-…"` or `habeas-example-…` anchors, on the badge itself.
- The nested-chapter test asserts `href="../requirements.html#habeas-req-requirements.ready"`.
- `examples_are_distinct_definitions_and_tests_link_to_them` asserts the same for an example.

**Fenced reference renders its badge followed by its body as Markdown.** `replace_references` emits a `habeas-fenced-ref` div with the badge, then the body, recursing on the body. The fenced-reference test asserts the badge comes before the body, the raw fence is gone, and nesting inside a `{req}` works.

**Fenced `{req}` and `{example}` render as a definition badge identifying the kind.** `replace_definitions` calls `shield_badge(block.kind.badge(), …)`.
- The example test asserts `alt="example requirements.something.foo"`.
- `shields_badge_urls_escape_requirement_names` checks the `req` badge URL and alt.

**Text outside a directive stays literal.**
- Invalid or unknown references, legacy inline `{req}` roles, invalid directive names and code-fenced examples are all left as written.
- These cases are asserted in `colon_directives_render_markdown_bodies_and_legacy_roles_stay_literal`, the fenced-reference test and the examples test.

**Visited-link legibility, focus indicator, hover, help cursor, inline layout and block styling.**
- `md/habeas.css` carries these (the requirement's `:impl:` option names it).
- `a.habeas-req-badge:visited` shares the rule that sets `color: inherit`.
- `:focus-visible` gets a 2px outline.
- `:hover` only brightens.
- `.habeas-builtin` gets a help cursor, `.habeas-req-badge` is `inline-flex`, and `.habeas-fenced-ref` is styled as a block.
- `badge_stylesheet_keeps_visited_links_legible_and_shows_focus` asserts the visited, focus and hover rules and that only Habeas selectors are styled.

The remaining behavior (the help cursor, inline layout, block styling, and `title` hover text for built-ins) is covered by the MAY clauses in the text. The `title` is asserted in the fenced-reference test.

text: :::{req} book_badges

In a book chapter, each valid `{impl}`, `{cite}`, or `{test}` reference, inline or fenced, MUST render as a Shields.io static badge image with meaningful alt text that displays its role and full name and links to the badge at the corresponding `{req}` or `{example}` definition. Links MUST work across chapters, including nested chapters. A fenced reference MUST render its badge followed by its body as Markdown. Each fenced `{req}` or `{example}` directive MUST render as a Shields.io definition badge image identifying its kind; text outside a directive MUST remain literal. Badge text MUST remain legible regardless of whether its link has been visited. A badge link MUST show a visible indicator when it has keyboard focus and MAY brighten on hover. Badges MAY be laid out inline with the surrounding text, a fenced reference's badge and body MAY be visually set apart from the surrounding text as one block, and a built-in's unlinked badge MAY show a help cursor to signal its hover text. These badges use the syntax defined by {cite}`requirements.references.roles`.
:::{req} roles

Project text files MAY use the `{impl}`, `{cite}`, and `{test}` roles with a backtick-delimited full requirement or example name, or with a built-in name under {cite}`requirements.references.builtin_definitions`, and MAY use the `{fixme}` role in fenced form. A reference MAY instead be written in fenced form, `:::{role} name` on one line, a body, and a closing fence, following the fence rules of {cite}`requirements.ci.span` and {cite}`requirements.ci.fence_lengths`; the fenced form is the same edge with attached commentary, and the inline form carries none. In a source comment, fence lines MUST be recognized after removing each line's comment delimiters within one comment run under {cite}`requirements.references.outline_comments`, and a fence that does not close within its comment run MUST be a validation error. Each reference is a directed edge between its source and the named definition. A source is a project source item or a requirement or example declaration. The roles MUST mean:
- `{cite}`: the source relies on, supports, or refers to the definition. It is an
edge from the source to the definition.
- `{impl}`: the source implements part of the definition: it makes a decision,
performs a check, produces an output, or handles a case that the definition
specifies. A requirement MAY implement part of another requirement by refining
one of its obligations. Calling code that implements a definition, or
producing a result a caller uses to meet it, MUST NOT by itself count as
implementing it. A check MUST count only if the definition states it, or the
source could not meet one of the definition's obligations without it; source
that checks it is consistent with a definition, such as recognizing a form the
definition specifies in order to decide whether to run other behavior, relies
on that definition and calls for `{cite}`. A requirement stating a convention
for every output of a kind, such as every validation error, is implemented by
the source that carries out the convention as a whole, such as the step that
collects and reports those outputs.
- `{test}`: the source is designed to verify behavior the definition specifies:
a test through its scenario and the assertions about that scenario's outcome,
or a named example through the concrete case it describes.
- `{fixme}`: the source acknowledges a known gap in fulfilling the definition. It
MUST use the fenced form, and its body MUST describe the gap. The body MAY
begin with option lines naming issues that track the gap, one per line, in the
form `:github: <owner>/<repo>#<number>`, such as
`:github: rust-lang/rust#123`. `github` MUST be the only recognized option.
A named `{fixme}` MAY appear only in sources outside the book. Validation MUST report
any other option line, a `:github:` value not in that form, an inline
`{fixme}`, a `{fixme}` in a requirement or example declaration, and a
`{fixme}` whose body, without option lines and comment delimiters, is empty.
An unnamed `{fixme}`, a fence of `:::{fixme}` with no name, MAY appear in any
project text, including a requirement or example body, to tie that place to
the issues it names. It MUST have at least one `:github:` option line and MAY
have a description; it is not a reference edge, acknowledges no gap, needs no
coverage, and does not count as a reference for Rust item coverage. Its
issues are checked under {cite}`requirements.cli.fixme_issues`.
`{impl}`, `{test}`, and `{fixme}` are edges from the definition to the source.
Only requirements and examples are assessed; code is reviewed as part of the
definitions it implements or tests.
```text
{impl}`requirements.references.roles`
{cite}`requirements.references.roles`
{test}`requirements.references.roles`
